Parent's note to the preschool, winter
Disha (5) has been scared of the dark since the long winter nights began. She says a monster lives in the cupboard. Last night she screamed when the power went out.
Her older brother Tenzin sat with her and opened the cupboard with a torch. "See? Only sweaters."
Disha peeked, then laughed. "Monster is pretend."
We have put a small night light in her room. She hugged me and slept. Please let us know if she mentions it at school.

qa.a: In the cupboard.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when the power went out?
qa.a: She felt frightened, screaming in the dark.

qa.q: What helped Disha separate the monster from reality?
qa.a: Tenzin opening the cupboard with a torch to show only sweaters, and a night light.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel after helping his sister?
qa.a: Tenzin likely feels proud and caring, glad she laughed.

grounding: A parent's note shows a young child learning a monster is pretend and accepting comfort.

On a hot summer night in their village, Nitin, five, refused to sleep on the roof with the family. "There's a ghost in the neem tree!"
His grandfather Thomas lay beside him and pointed. "That's the wind moving the leaves. Listen."
Nitin listened. Rustle, rustle.
"And the white thing?"
"The moon on the branch."
Nitin held Thomas's hand tight, watching the tree. Slowly his grip loosened. He fell asleep counting stars.

qa.q: What did Nitin think was in the neem tree?
qa.a: A ghost.

qa.q: How was Nitin feeling at first?
qa.a: He felt scared, refusing to sleep on the roof.

qa.q: How did Thomas help Nitin?
qa.a: He lay beside him and explained what the sounds and shapes really were.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel as Nitin's grip loosens?
qa.a: Thomas probably feels relieved and tender.

grounding: Shows a young child separating imagined ghosts from reality with a grandparent's comfort.

His mother Yara came with a lamp. Thunder rolled. A branch scratched the glass.
"Look," she said, lifting the curtain. "It's the mango branch."

He nodded, snuggling into her. "Stay till I sleep?"

Monday: Pallavi, ten, stared at her science chapter on the water cycle. She read it three times and still couldn't remember the order. She felt stupid.

passage:
Zeenat, you're struggling with your tables? Let me tell you how I learned mine, during one monsoon when I was nine.
I, Nikita, couldn't remember eight times anything. My father made me write them again and again. Nothing stuck.
Then it rained for a week, and school closed. My grandmother sat with me on the veranda and turned the tables into songs. Every morning we sang the eights. Every evening, before dinner, she asked me three, just three.
After a week I could do them. After a month I knew them in my sleep.
So, Zeenat, a little every day, and sing it. Don't stuff it all in one night.

qa.q: What did Nikita's grandmother turn the tables into?
qa.a: Songs.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel when nothing stuck?
qa.a: Nikita felt frustrated and discouraged, writing the tables again and again.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Nikita's story?
qa.a: The grandmother singing the tables every morning and asking three every evening, a little each day.

qa.q: How might Nikita's grandmother have felt as the tables stuck?
qa.a: She likely felt proud and happy that her songs worked.

grounding: An elder recalls learning with repetition, songs and spaced review as a child.

passage:
On the day before the winter exams, the power went out in Asif's building. He had planned to reread his whole history book that night.
His friend Anirban came over with a torch. "You can't read 80 pages by torch. Just do your summary cards."
Asif had made small cards every week: one date, one event, one reason. He had almost forgotten them.
They sat on the steps with the torch, testing each other. Asif got the ones he'd reviewed often right, and the new ones wrong. He put the wrong ones in a separate pile and went through them again.
By ten, he knew most of them. The lights came back. He didn't open the book.

qa.q: What was on each summary card?
qa.a: One date, one event, one reason.

qa.q: How might Asif have felt when the power went out?
qa.a: He likely felt worried and panicky, since he had planned to reread the whole book.

qa.q: Why did the summary cards work better than rereading?
qa.a: They held key points in small pieces, let him test himself, and focused on the ones he got wrong.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel helping by torchlight?
qa.a: Anirban probably feels pleased and useful, enjoying quizzing his friend.

grounding: Shows a child using summaries, repetition and self-testing under pressure.

In the Class 5 maths room, Swati slammed her pencil down. "I can't do fractions. I'm just bad at maths."
Ramesh sir pulled up a chair. "Can't, or can't yet?"

"Remember in Class 3 when you couldn't do long division?"

Day one, she fell nine times. She said "I'll never learn" and cried. I told her it was normal.
Day three, she fell less, and said, "I can't do turns. Not yet."
Day six, she was going around the rink, wobbly, grinning at every corner.

Irawati, you're stuck on that riddle? Come, I'll tell you how I learned to solve these, when I was ten.
I, Vikas, a skinny boy of ten, loved riddles but hated maths. My uncle gave me this one: a man has three sons, each son has one sister. How many children?
I shouted "six!" He laughed. "Slow down. Draw it."
I drew three boys. Then one sister for each. Then I saw: the same sister. Four children.
After that I drew every puzzle. Step by step, no shouting answers. My maths got better too.
So, Irawati, get a pencil. Draw it.

"Next number: 2, 4, 8, 16, ..." Rashmi read.

Preeti, you want to know why I write letters to the newspaper? It started when I was eleven, during the Pongal holidays.

passage:
Harsha, you're curious about my garden? Let me tell you how it started, one summer when I was nine.
I, Rehana, a curious girl, guessed that plants grow faster with music. My brother laughed. So I planted two pots of beans. One on the window with the radio, one on the window without.
Every day I measured with a ruler and wrote it down.
After two weeks, they were the same height. I was so disappointed.
My father said, "You found something out. That's science."
So, Harsha, guess. Test. And don't be sad if you were wrong.

qa.q: What did Rehana plant?
qa.a: Two pots of beans.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when both plants were the same height?
qa.a: Rehana felt disappointed.

qa.q: What was the lesson inside Rehana's story?
qa.a: Her father's point that finding out, even if the guess was wrong, is science.

qa.q: How might Rehana's brother have felt after the result?
qa.a: The brother may have felt smug but also curious about Rehana's careful test.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood experiment, testing a guess and accepting the result.

passage:
During the Diwali holidays, Leela, eleven, wanted to test which diya burned longest: one with ghee or one with oil. Her cousin Ganga said oil.
Then the wind blew out both diyas halfway through. Leela almost gave up.
Instead she moved the test indoors, relit them at the same time, and checked the clock every ten minutes.
The ghee diya lasted longer. Ganga frowned. "Maybe the wick was different."
Leela thought. "Good point. Tomorrow we use the same wick."

qa.q: What blew out both diyas?
qa.a: The wind.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when the diyas blew out?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and nearly gave up.

qa.q: What made Leela's test fair?
qa.a: She moved it indoors, relit both together, checked the clock, and planned to use the same wick.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel when Leela takes her point seriously?
qa.a: Ganga likely feels respected and interested.

grounding: Shows a child running a fair experiment despite complications.
